title: Guard rails and the kill switch
summary: Batch 3: nine guard rails (G1 to G9) for short-lived deployments and the daily region move, and four choices (K1 to K4) for the Vault cost kill switch; drafted by ec2.aws.a, reviewed by security.aws.a. Lower-bound list prices; approving creates nothing in AWS.

beats.narration: Nine guard rails and four kill-switch choices. Approving them creates nothing in AWS.
G1. Recommended: two hours by default, four as the hard cap.
G2. Recommended: each daily-move copy capped at 26 hours, as a backstop.
G3. Recommended: London and Ireland only, the two priced today.
G4. Recommended: the three smallest Graviton types, standard credits.
G5. Recommended: three at once at most, a low vCPU quota behind it.
G6. Recommended: alert at 25 dollars. Whether it also stops new deployments is your pick.
G7. Recommended: stop new in one click; end all only with your approval.
G8. Recommended: the sweeper as a scheduled function in our account.
G9. Recommended: a week of daily moves in the twin before any real move.
K1. Recommended: the automatic pause opt-in, off by default. A flood can then switch a Vault off.
K2. Recommended: throttle and disable the distribution.
K3. Recommended: a fast alarm over five minutes and a slow one over six hours.
K4. Recommended: the same switch on for our own deployments.
All a, except G1, a plus b, G9, b then a, and K1 and K2, b. Answer in pm.aws.a's session.

visual.caption: Recommended: G1 a+b, G2 a, G3 a, G4 a, G5 a, G6 a with (i) or (ii), G7 a, G8 a, G9 b then a, K1 b, K2 b, K3 both alarms (45,000 per 5 min, 44,121 per 6 h), K4 yes

decisions.question: G1. How long a short-lived deployment may live?
decisions.why: Recommended: a+b. Default (a) 2 hours, hard cap (b) 4 hours. Costs at most 0.0476 and 0.0952 USD (t4g.small plus a public IPv4). Security: the lifetime tag is set only at launch; no role can change it.

decisions.question: G2. How long each daily-move copy may live?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a) 26 h: 0.6188 USD a copy at the cap; 17.37 USD always on for a month. Past 26 h the sweeper alerts first and deletes a copy only once its replacement answers.

decisions.question: G3. Which regions are allowed?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a) now; (b) by a later decision once billing prices them and the twin tests them. Security: the region condition applies to regional actions only.

decisions.question: G4. Which instance types are allowed?

options.label: a. nano, micro, small (0.0047 to 0.0188/h USD)

decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a); medium only if the twin load test says so. Standard credits checked by the test suite and in the plan read-back.

decisions.question: G5. How many at once?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a). A runaway loop is the main cost risk. The vCPU quota is an AWS change of its own, and account-wide.

decisions.question: G6. The monthly cost alert?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. At the cap: (i) alert only, recommended by security.aws.a; (ii) alert plus an automatic stop new (Budgets action, deletes nothing, undone by detaching the policy), recommended by ec2.aws.a. Your pick. New (billing.aws.a, ddddb44): a request flood through CloudFront is billed per request at the edge, about $46 an hour at 10,000 requests a second in London, so a $25 alert would be reached within an hour; billing is pricing an edge rate limit (AWS WAF) and a billing alarm.

decisions.question: G7. The kill switch?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a): deleting stacks is not undone by pressing again. Clearing stop new is also a plan you approve.

decisions.question: G8. Where the sweeper runs?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. (a). Each deployment also gets its own one-time delete schedule. The sweeper may only describe, alert and delete managed sws-ec2-* stacks.

decisions.question: G9. When the daily move starts?
decisions.why: Recommended: b then a. (b) first, then (a). Order fixed: the new copy answers, DNS moves, then the old copy is deleted. The move's role holds no key.

decisions.question: K1. Offer the automatic pause??
decisions.why: Recommended: b. (b): a flood then costs about one evaluation period plus propagation; one pause per flood, no automatic restore. Trade-off: anyone who can send enough requests can switch a Vault off.

decisions.question: K2. Which levers the pause pulls?
decisions.why: Recommended: b. (b): CloudFront is 43.20 of 45.89 USD an hour in a flood at 10,000 req/s.

decisions.question: K3. The suggested thresholds?

options.label: a. Fast alarm: 45,000 requests in 5 minutes (about $1 an hour)
good: Stops a big flood within minutes
bad: Alone, a flood held just under it cost $729 in 30 days

options.label: b. Slow alarm: 44,121 requests in 6 hours (from $10 a month)
bad: Just over it, up to about $12.41 before the switch acts

decisions.why: Recommended: both a and b, billing's figures suggested; the customer decides. Two alarms: fast 45,000 requests in 5 minutes (about $1 an hour); slow 44,121 in 6 hours, from a $10-a-month budget (billing.aws.a, 7621a65). Held under both: at most about $10 a month; just over the slow one: up to about $12.41 before the switch acts. With the fast alarm alone, a flood held just under it cost $729 in 30 days (27911d0).

decisions.question: K4. The same switch on our own deployments?
decisions.why: Recommended: a. Part of the guard rails; restore is a plan you approve.
